catalog_quote: Most of the variation in stress assignment results from the interaction of a general penultimate stress target with a constraint requiring stress to be placed foot initially, with feet mostly constructed to align with morphemes, but with some additional specific constraints. Light syllables sometimes also optionally reject stress and compounds and certain types of suffixes form new right edges at their boundaries, allowing more than one primary stress to be assigned. Overall, this leads to stress falling anywhere between the last syllable (in monosyllables) and the fifth-last (in the irrealis form of some verbs). ... word stress can fall on the penultimate syllable because it is foot-initial (which in the unmarked case follows from being morpheme initial) ... sweep_summary: One sweep item only: Bishop 2002 (Melbourne PhD, Glottolog 5771, already listed). Minerva bot-blocked live fetches today, the handle still redirects to it); text layer present, no scanned needed. Read §1.4.4, §3.4, §3.7, §3.11, §3.13. Chapter 3 is a first-hand metrical analysis of Kuninjku and Manyallaluk Mayali word stress/accent: left-headed unbounded feet aligned to morpheme left edges (each morpheme = one foot except cohering morphemes), no lexical accent, limited quantity sensitivity, initial stress on mono-morphemic roots, Kuninjku default single accent on the leftmost foot (End Rule Left), MM default accent on the root's foot plus an optional penultimate foot boundary. This confirms the catalog's 'morphological' classification and refines it (dialect-specific default accent; the penultimate target of Evans's Gun-Djeihmi/Kundedjnjenghmi description is derived, not positional). It does not supersede Evans 2003, whose principles Bishop explicitly adapts. line added at Nothing left to acquire. Note: the directory also holds non-sweep companions fetched sources on 9/16 (Bishop 2002 Speech Prosody paper, Bishop & Fletcher 2005 OUP chapter scanned, Mansfield 2022 OSF preprint) that were not items in this sweep and were not re-read.

new_statements.quote: As described in Chapter 1 (§1.4.4), feet are left-headed and unbounded in all dialects of BGW. BGW displays quantity sensitivity only in limited circumstances (see §3.6), and has no lexical accent [...] In BGW, the construction of metrical constituents makes reference to the left edge of the morpheme, which is constrained to align with the left edge of a foot (Evans, 1995; in press). [...] Feet are left-headed and unbounded. The left edge of a morpheme must align with the left edge of a foot; therefore: Each morpheme minimally corresponds to a single foot, with the exception of a set of cohering morphemes, which form a foot together with the preceding morpheme.

new_statements.reading: Stress placement in Bininj Gun-wok is morphologically governed: each morpheme (minus cohering ones) forms one unbounded left-headed foot, so stress falls on morpheme-initial syllables; which foot carries the word's single default pitch accent is dialect-specific (Kuninjku: leftmost foot/word-initial; Manyallaluk Mayali: the root's foot, generally rightmost, with an optional extra penultimate foot), and the 'penultimate' primary stress reported for Gun-Djeihmi/Kundedjnjenghmi is the derived outcome of root-final footing rather than a positional rule. This confirms the catalog's 'morphological' coding and refines it with dialect-specific default-accent rules and the quantity-sensitivity/emphatic-accent exceptions.

sources.citation: Bishop, Judith. 2002. Aspects of intonation and prosody in Bininj Gun-wok: an autosegmental-metrical analysis. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics and Applied Linguistics, University of Melbourne. 476 pp. (PDF 510 pp. with front matter). Glottolog ref 5771; OZBIB 514.
sources.quote: The data presented in this chapter demonstrate that the location of pitch accents in BGW words is basically conditioned by metrical structure, which is calculated on the basis of morphological structure within the morphosyntactic word. [...] In Kuninjku, a default single accent typically associates with the head of the leftmost foot in a polypedal phonological word, and a second accent generally associates with the rightmost foot. In Manyallaluk Mayali, a default single accent associates with the root of the morphosyntactic word, however, again, a second accent seeks out a word-peripheral foot: the leftmost foot.
sources.note: Primarily an intonation thesis, but Chapter 3 (pp.111-211) is a full first-hand metrical analysis of word stress/accent in the Kuninjku and Manyallaluk Mayali (MM) dialects. Bishop adopts and slightly reformulates Evans's foot-construction principles: feet are left-headed and unbounded in all dialects; the left edge of every morpheme must align with the left edge of a foot, so each morpheme is minimally one foot, except a set of cohering morphemes that foot together with the preceding morpheme (pp.119-120); BGW has no lexical accent and only limited quantity sensitivity (§3.6: a closed second…

sources.quote: '[BGW] has conventionally been described as a stress language (Evans 1995; Fletcher and Evans 2000) with no lexical use of pitch. Its polysynthetic structure results in complex metrical stress rules (see Evans (1995, 2003) and Bishop (2001, 2003: ch. 3) for a more detailed treatment than can be given here). Pitch accents can anchor to more than one metrically strong syllable within the word: a single morphosyntactic word may carry two to three pitch accents.'
sources.note: Cross-dialect intonation survey (six dialects incl. Manyallaluk Mayali, which Evans says does not follow his rules); defers to Evans 2003/Bishop 2002 ch.3 for the stress rules.
